title: Florissant CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Florissant wells have a 280 ft median depth and 5 gpm median yield. See local drilling costs, water levels, and risks before you buy or build.
h1: Water wells in the Florissant, Colorado area
intro_html:
If you are looking at land or a home on a well around Florissant, the state records give a decent picture of what to expect. Within about five miles there are 3,773 well permits, with 2,639 reporting total depth and 1,610 reporting pump yield, all in fractured mountain bedrock.

Below is what those wells say about typical depths, production, costs, and risks for this part of Teller County, including nearby Divide, Lake George, and Woodland Park.

sections.heading: How deep wells run around Florissant
sections.html:
In the Florissant area, most wells are drilled into fractured granite and similar bedrock, so depth can vary a lot from one property to the next. The median reported total depth is 280 feet, and the middle half of wells land between 151 and 400 feet. About 42% of wells fall in the 100–300 foot range, and another 42% are 300–600 feet, so a driller will usually bid assuming something in that broad window.

There are shallow successes, with 9% under 100 feet, but you also see deep holes: 10% of wells go deeper than 520 feet and the deepest on record hits 1,100 feet. When you price land, assume you might need more than the 280-foot median unless nearby wells on similar ground tell a consistent story.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Production in this fractured-bedrock zone is modest but usually workable for a household. The median reported yield is 5.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells fall between 1.5 and 9.0 gpm. About 49% of wells report between 5 and 15 gpm, which is plenty for typical domestic use under the 35 gpm exempt-well pumping limit.

The concern is the lower end: 14% of wells test under 1 gpm and 33% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. Those can still serve a home if you manage storage and use, but they are not generous. When you evaluate a specific lot, pay close attention to yields on adjacent or nearby wells rather than just assuming you will hit the 5 gpm median.

sections.heading: Water levels and what the trend suggests
sections.html:
Static water level is how far down the water sits in the casing when the well is at rest. Around Florissant, 215 wells report this, with a current median of 100 feet below ground, and the middle half between 70 and 145 feet. That means your pump will usually sit well below 100 feet, even if the total hole is much deeper.

By decade, median depth to water has bounced around: about 88 feet in the 1970s, 45 feet in the 1980s, 85 feet in the 2010s, and 115 feet in the 2020s. That points to a water table that is variable and lately somewhat deeper than in earlier records. When you buy, look at the date and water level on nearby wells to see if more recent completions are showing deeper water than older ones.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling around Florissant
sections.html:
State records show steady well development around Florissant and nearby places like Divide and Lake George. Permits start showing up in small numbers in the 1950s (20 permits) and 1960s (52), then jump sharply: 546 in the 1970s, 692 in the 1980s, and a peak of 993 in the 1990s. Activity slows after that, with 584 permits in the 2000s, 252 in the 2010s, and 207 already in the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025.

Drilling is dominated by a few outfits in the records: Mountain Well Improvement LLC (586 wells), Woods Drilling Inc. (560), and RMPD, Ltd dba Rocky Mtn Pump & Drilling (420). When you shop drillers, it helps to ask who has actually drilled in your immediate area and to review completion reports from those specific companies.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
Florissant sits on fractured mountain bedrock, mainly granite and gneiss, which usually means air-rotary drilling at a per-foot rate. The typical range in this area is about $65–$100 per foot. At the local median depth of 280 feet, that puts the drilled hole itself in the ballpark of $18,200–$28,000 before you add hardware and hookups.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a complete working well at that same median depth often totals around $24,200–$40,000. If your site or geology pushes you toward the deeper end of the local range, say closer to the 400–520 foot bracket, costs climb accordingly. Get bids that clearly separate drilling footage from completion items so you understand what is driving the number.

sections.heading: Local risks: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
In this fractured-bedrock setting, the biggest practical risk is low yield: 14% of wells report under 1 gpm and another 33% are between 1 and 5 gpm. Those wells can be made to work with storage, but they change how you size pumps and tanks and may affect resale value. There are also mapped environmental concerns within about 10 miles: 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 34 historic mine features, and 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup locations.

That does not mean your specific well is polluted, but it is a reason to budget for a good lab test panel on any existing well. When planning a new build, keep proper separation from septic and leach fields and pay attention to slopes and access for drill rigs and trenching machines on this mountain terrain.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot near Florissant
sections.html:
Most permits around Florissant are domestic or household use (94%), with only small shares for stock (4%) and monitoring (1%), so the data set lines up well with typical home sites. Before you commit to a parcel, pull the well permits and completion reports for the closest properties and note reported depths, yields, and static water levels.

Lots that already have a well with a documented 5 gpm or better yield and a reasonable depth near the 280-foot median are often safer bets than raw land. On vacant ground, talk with a local well contractor about specific risks for your lot compared to nearby Divide, Lake George, or Cripple Creek. Pair that with a realistic drilling and septic budget so the total project cost does not surprise you after closing.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around Florissant, Colorado?
faq.a: State records within about five miles of Florissant show a median well depth of 280 feet, with the middle half of wells between 151 and 400 feet. About 42% of wells are 100–300 feet deep and another 42% are 300–600 feet. Around 10% go deeper than 520 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,100 feet.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Florissant, CO?
faq.a: Reported pump yields near Florissant have a median of 5.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 1.5 and 9.0 gpm. Roughly 49% of wells produce 5–15 gpm, which is comfortable for most households. However, 14% of wells come in under 1 gpm and 33% are between 1 and 5 gpm, so low-yield wells are a real possibility.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Florissant?
faq.a: The limited static water level data show some variation over time. Median depth to water was about 88 feet in the 1970s, 45 feet in the 1980s, then around 85 feet in the 2010s and 115 feet in the 2020s. That suggests water levels have been deeper in more recent measurements than in earlier decades, but with only 215 wells reporting, it is a coarse indicator.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Florissant?
faq.a: In the fractured granite and gneiss around Florissant, typical drilling runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the local median depth of 280 feet, the drilled hole alone pencils out roughly $18,200–$28,000. A complete system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals about $24,200–$40,000, with deeper wells costing more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in the Florissant area?
faq.a: Records show mapped risks in the broader area, including 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 34 historic mine features, and 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Many private wells are fine, but quality can vary by location. For any existing well, plan on a comprehensive lab test for bacteria, metals, and, where relevant, PFAS before relying on it for drinking water.
